Row.Text: Babylon is remembered today as a city of beauty, culture, and sometimes decadence. It started though as a small and inconsequential city-state, founded around four thousand years ago. The great king Hammurabi rose to power around 1700 BCE and spread Babylonian culture across Southern Mesopotamia in what we refer to as the Old Babylonian Empire. Though immensely impactful thanks to the political, cultural, and scientific developments of Hammurabi and his astronomers, this phase of Babylon’s power was short-lived. After Hammurabi died, the empire quickly collapsed and Babylon retreated to less important status, changing hands over the centuries from one neighbor to another. Its cultural impact, however, remained supreme and maintaining hold over Babylon was a sign of prestige even as the city fought continually for independence.

Come the seventh century BCE, the great Assyrian Empire of the north had turned its gaze on Babylon. King Sennacherib besieged Babylon for fifteen months, eventually sacking it and destroying much of its beauty. After his assassination at the hands of his sons, his successor Ashurhaddon rebuilt Babylon and sent many of its people home. The relationship between Assyria and Babylon was complex. Rather than empires of different peoples who supplanted each other, they were closely related culturally. Much of Assyria's culture had been adapted from Old Babylonian culture, and both states spoke the same languages (Akkadian and Aramaic, the first giving way to the second throughout the period). Both worshipped the same pantheon, though each prioritized different deities. Though Assyria was strong and Babylon weak militarily at this time, Assyria had a deep respect and appreciation for Babylonian culture. Sennacherib’s crime against the city may have contributed to his demise.

In 631 BCE, when the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal died, his kingdom fell into a period of disarray, and Babylon saw an opportunity. A local man named Nabopolassar rose up in rebellion against the Assyrian general in control of the region and successfully overthrew him. Nabopolassar was crowned king and Babylon was independent once more. Seeing the weakness of Assyria, he pushed forward, eventually allying with the nearby Medes and together taking city by city across Mesopotamia. In 612, Assyria’s capital Nineveh fell to the Medo-Babylonian forces, marking the beginning of the end of the Assyrian Empire. By 605, Nabopolassar had conquered his only rival Egypt and supplanted the old Assyrian lands with what we now refer to as the Neo-Babylonian Empire, or in some places, the Chaldean Empire. Alas, he died before he could enjoy the fruits of his conquest.

Nebuchadnezzar II succeeded Nabopolassar, and much of the beauty of Babylon we think of today is owed to his reign. Though he did pursue several military campaigns including his well-known conquest of the Levant (and captivity of the Jewish people as recounted in the Hebrew Bible), he is most remembered as a great builder who brought Babylon to the peak of its power and grandeur, and spread Babylonian culture and renown throughout the Mesopotamian valley. Babylonian kingship claimed much of its royal stature from its ability to pursue building projects. The practice dates back to at least the successors of Hammurabi whose inscriptions lived on in the old foundations of the building they had constructed. In Nebuchadnezzar’s time, his renovations involved digging down to the original foundations, finding said inscriptions, and placing both an offering and his own inscription in the same place. In addition, he restored and built palaces, temples, streets, canals and other infrastructure, using more resilient materials and marking them with his name. The most famous of his projects (aside from the probably mythical Hanging Gardens) is perhaps the Ishtar Gate, one of the northern gates into the inner city of Babylon. The gate was covered in blue glazed bricks of a deep indigo and featured reliefs of various animals who were sacred to Babylonian deities – dragons for Marduk and lions for Ishtar, among others. Pieces of the gate were excavated in the 20th century, and a reconstructed version of the gate can be seen today in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.

Aside from monuments and buildings, Nebuchadnezzar is also responsible for a thriving economy centered on the city of Babylon, the capital of the world at this point. The vassal states from across his empire contributed tribute and Babylonian merchants developed a rich trade network into Anatolia, to Egypt, and east into Iran. Seafaring merchants, especially Phoenicians, had positions in Nebuchadnezzar’s court, showing both the extent of Babylonian trade and the cosmopolitan fabric of the city. The earliest records of banking activities date to this time with key Babylonian families, especially the Egibis, participating in lending, investment, and real estate. Non-Babylonians were also frequently traders, craftsmen, and farmers, and Nebuchadnezzar brought many of his subjected peoples into the city as prisoners to build his great projects. Many ethnicities and languages were present in Babylon, both free and in servitude, possibly contributing to the story of the Tower of Babel, a mythologized story of Babylon’s architectural hubris (from the perspective of the empire’s subjects) and multicultural reality.

Nebuchadnezzar died in 562 BCE, leaving an unsure succession that devolved into a series of coups. The empire never recovered, and a new threat emerged – Cyrus the soon-to-be Great, leader of the Persians. The last king of Babylon, Nabonidus, did little to prepare for the coming showdown. In 539 BCE, after only a single military encounter outside the city, Babylon fell to the Persians. Nabonidus was captured and exiled. Babylon would never again rise as an independent power.

Though Babylon fell to Persian rule, it remained a city of glory under Cyrus the Great and was the place of the winter residence of the Achaemenids until their eventual fall. Thanks to Cyrus’ policies of tolerance, the city flourished and remained an economic center through the Persian period and long after it was captured by Alexander the Great in 333 BCE. It was not until the seventh century CE that Babylon would begin to decline and by the 13th century, it had become only a small village and lost relevance for centuries. In the modern day, it found new life under Saddam Hussein who, in the Babylonian style of kingship, was determined to rebuild the glory of the city. Though his plans for a new Hanging Gardens never materialized, he did leave a portrait of himself and King Nebuchadnezzar with an inscription that mimicked Nebuchadnezzar’s style and named Hussein as Nebuchadnezzar's son. Today, it is a World Heritage Site and many villages populate the old city’s area.

Like many of the Mesopotamian cultures in Antiquity, Babylonian kings and elites enjoyed the presence of nature for contemplation and relaxation. These pleasure gardens, the kirimāḫu, were typically located outside of the palace but still within the surrounding grounds. Some cities had larger-scale gardens located in the outskirts that functioned more like a wildlife park and botanical garden, the most famous example of which was in Nineveh, the capital of Assyria that fell to the Babylonians in 612 BCE. In Babylon’s city center, we know of one specific space called the “Juniper Garden” (kirî burāši) that was situated between two temples and enclosed a library and “House of Deliberation,” among other structures.

The water required for these gardens was channeled through a complex network of canals that transported water from the Euphrates River. Evidence for these canals dates back to the mid-2nd millennium BCE in the Old Babylonian period, showing the advanced engineering skills Babylon developed to support the agricultural needs of its population and later the aesthetic desires of its elites.

The Euphrates River, Purattu in Akkadian, flowed through the city of Babylon and, along with the Tigris River, was integral to the irrigation system that supplied the gardens and farms of the surrounding region. Evidence for irrigation in the Euphrates basin dates back to as early as 6000 BCE, though the complex systems of transporting and raising water via canals and mechanisms only developed in the region in the first millennium BCE.

Canals began with a muballitum, a structure made of wood and reeds that provided the means to control the amount of water flowing from the river into the canal. Valves were placed along the canals to provide outlets for managing water levels. Lifts and wheels were used in some cases to raise water to higher levels. In Diodorus’ account describing the Hanging Gardens, he mentions these mechanisms and says they were hidden within the walls so that water could reach the highest terraces without any visitor seeing the machinery.

From as early as the third millennium BCE, Babylonians celebrated Akitu, a festival or series of festivals, at the beginning of their new year, the start of spring and the sowing season, and at the start of autumn. Babylon would fill with visitors from neighboring towns and cities, and trade flowed amidst the religious activities and general festive atmosphere. Many new harrānu, business partnerships, were formed during Akitu, as it was one of the best opportunities of the year to meet new partners and create new trade ventures.

Festivities during Akitu took place across the city, focused on the Esagila, the temple of Marduk, where the high priest began and ended the festival. Throughout the 12-day celebration, priests conducted a series of rituals involving the king and various Babylonian gods who paid their respects to Marduk. The epic Enuma Elish was recited and Marduk’s victory over Tiamat reenacted symbolically. At one point, the king was ritually humiliated in the temple of Marduk, to prove his loyalty to Marduk. The priest would strike the king on the cheek, hoping for tears as these were a good omen. A similar ritual occurred in the autumn celebration when the king was ritually imprisoned overnight and restored to his position the next morning.

Akitu was celebrated throughout the Mesopotamian valley into the first millennium CE. In the 20th century, it was resurrected as an Assyrian New Year and is celebrated still today across the diaspora of Assyrians, Chaldeans, and Arameans, and within Iraq on April 1st. Individuals wear traditional clothing or dress up as Assyrian royalty, and women create garlands to hang on their homes’ front doors – the “Beard of April” that welcomes spring.

The great Babylonian creation myth, Enuma Elish, tells the story of how the cosmos came to be, how Marduk fought with the other gods and became the highest, how he made man and the earth, and how Babylon was built for him. Our earliest manuscript was recovered from Nineveh in the 19th century and dates to the ninth century BCE. The poem’s composition came a few centuries earlier, most likely during the Second Dynasty of Isin (c. 1155-1026 BCE) when Marduk had achieved his position as head of the pantheon. Before Marduk, Enlil was head of the gods and spoke to his followers through Marduk and Ishtar, the other important deity of Babylon. Though she plays only a minor role in Enuma Elish, other poetry gives her a primary place, such as the Descent of Ishtar, the Hymns of Agushaya and Ammī-ditāna, and, of course, the Sumerian Epic of Gilgamesh.

Enuma Elish is composed of about a thousand lines of non-rhyming couplets, written in cuneiform across seven clay tablets. Its content holds many similarities to other creation myths, including that found in the Book of Genesis, though several differences disallow a strict interpretation of direct inspiration. The battle between Tiamat and Marduk shows many borrowings from the Anzû myth and the story of creation is similar to that found in the Enūma Anu Enlil, the Babylonian astrological text. Man is created from the combination of bone and the blood of a murdered god, recalling similarities to the Orphic myth of the origin of man and hinting at the Mesopotamian influences on Greek myth.

The Babylonian economy of the Neo-Babylonian period, particularly during the long sixth century, was at the height of its growth. Standard of living among Babylonian citizens rose sharply during this period as urbanization and enterprise created a virtuous loop of economic growth. The period has been termed a “golden interval” by scholars of Babylon, the term originally coined by the economist J. Maynard Keynes to describe such rare occurrences of economic prosperity in the pre-industrial world.

The relative stability that Babylon brought to the region after its conquest of the Assyrian Empire helped provide the conditions needed for economic growth. The region’s climate in the period was also in a state of health – there was more moisture and the river system was more consistent across the Euphrates and Tigris basin. As agricultural production became more efficient, population levels rose. Laborers moved into the city and began to specialize. Much of the workforce was composed of freemen, mār banê, paid a wage in silver for their labor. Consumption patterns changed as well. We see dowries become more valuable and houses start to contain higher quality goods constructed from materials that would have been out of reach for much more of the population in the previous century. The state invested in infrastructure, supporting the growing economy, and a system of private land ownership and private enterprise provided a continual market of opportunities. Some economic historians consider this period of Babylonian history an example of early capitalism. The golden interval, however, did not last. After the Persian conquest of Babylon, the city remained a key commercial center but failed to continue its trajectory of growth as revolts and unrest interrupted much of the stability that had allowed the city to prosper.

The Babylonian tamkāru (or professional merchant) was a key element of the rich and broad economy that the Babylonian Empire enjoyed throughout both the Old and Neo-Babylonian periods. There were both civilian tamkāru and royal tamkāru (tamkār šarri), both of whom participated in activities like lending, logistics, long-distance trade, and local buying and selling of goods, real estate, and slaves. Tamkāru traded a variety of goods - precious metals, building supplies, food, luxuries, etc. across Mesopotamia, Anatolia, and into Egypt and modern-day Iran.

Though many of the most well-established tamkāru were from Babylonian families, both groups of tamkāru could be Babylonian or non-Babylonian, including even individuals from captive territories like Judah. These foreign-born tamkāru were more likely to be involved in long-distance trade which provided opportunities for them to connect their place of origin more closely with the capital and likely played a key role in expanding the Babylonian trade network.

Babylonian archers, or qašti (lit: (men) of the bow), were primarily sourced from temples during times of war. In Babylonian society, the military was predominantly composed of men who had full-time roles in society outside of active military campaigns, and this was true for temple archers as well. Should it be peacetime, these men would have been employed as shepherds, farmers, or other such roles as temples had control over lands and required significant manpower to care for the temple and support its people. Many of these individuals were originally prisoners taken in war who were given to temples as workers and thus had little choice in their tasks.

The qašti were organized in decuries according to the men's peacetime role - a decury of shepherds, of gardeners, etc., and the command was given to a rab qašti, chief of the archers. Their bows were of both the Akkadian (slow but forceful) and Cimmerian (rapid fire) composite styles, and bowmakers were employed by the temple to craft and repair the qašti’s weaponry. They would have also been equipped with daggers, made by the temple’s smiths, and given a supply of about 50 arrows for which they were responsible.
